title: Toe Walking as a Primary Clinical Indicator of PMP22 Mutation-Associated Neuropathies in Children
summary:
Toe Walking in Children – Could It Be a Sign of an Inherited Nerve Disorder? 
What is this study about?
Some children walk on their toes for a long time without any clear reason, like muscle weakness or developmental delays. This study wanted to find out if this so-called "idiopathic toe walking" might be linked to genetic changes—especially in the PMP22 gene, which plays a role in certain nerve disorders.
 How was the study done? 
- 24 children who were examined had frequently walked on their toes since an early age. 
-In all children included in our study, a genetic analysis was performed to screen for variations in the 49 genes of a tip-toe walking panel associated with neuropathies.
- They also had physical exams to look for related issues, such as foot deformities (like high arches) or balance problems. 
What did the study find?
-For our study, we selected all children who actually had genetic variants in the PMP22 gene.
- Nearly all children had additional physical signs, including: 
      - High foot arches (92%)
      - Spinal issues (exaggerated lower back curve, 92%) 
      -Tremors or speech difficulties (in about half of them) 
- In nearly half of the cases, there were reports of family members with similar problems, suggesting a hereditary predisposition
Why does this matter ?
The study suggests that persistent toe walking may not just be a harmless habit- it could be an early sign of an inherited nerve disorder.
If a child still walks on their toes often after age 2,  genetic testing might help identify the cause early and guide proper treatment.
What does this mean for affected families?
- Parents whose child often walks on their toes should talk to a pediatrician, neurologist, or orthopedist. 
- If other family members have similar issues, genetic counseling can help assess risks for future children. 
- Early physical therapy or orthopedic support may help prevent long-term foot or posture problems. 
In short: This study shows that toe walking in children can sometimes be an early clue to an inherited nerve disorder. Genetic testing may help uncover the cause and ensure children get the right care.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Toe walking for more than half of the day
Completion of a specific genetic test using a panel of 49 genes
Exclusion criteria:
absence of neurological/orthopedic conditions, such as cerebral palsy, autism spectrum disorder, tethered cord syndrome, children with birth complications, severe orthopedic deformities including limb length discrepancies, scoliosis or severe foot deformities.
